title: Urinary Organs: Location and Boundaries
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter places the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra in the body and names what surrounds each one. It covers renal position and relations, the renal coverings and hilum, the course and narrow points of the ureter, the bladder trigone and urethral segments, and the anatomy of male urethral injury. Board questions rarely ask for a relation as a bare fact. They describe flank pain moving toward the groin, fluid in a recess on imaging, recurrent cystitis in a young woman, or blood at the urethral meatus after trauma, and ask you to reason back to the structure involved.
prerequisites: The peritoneum, peritoneal cavity, and the difference between intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal organs
Muscles of the posterior abdominal wall and vertebral level landmarks such as the transpyloric plane (L1)
Internal gross structure of the kidney: cortex, medulla, calyces, and renal pelvis (UR-1)
Urothelium and the layers of the ureter and bladder wall (UR-2)
Layers of the perineum: perineal membrane, deep and superficial perineal pouches, and the membranous layer of superficial fascia

connections.how: The duodenum, pancreas, and colic flexures lie directly on the kidneys, so disease and injury cross between the two systems.

connections.to: Urinary system in the abdominopelvic cavity (UR-4)
connections.how: The relations here set the stage for the renal vessels, the bladder's position in the pelvis, and the peritoneal recesses around the urinary organs.
The prostate surrounds the first part of the male urethra, and the ductus deferens and uterine artery cross the pelvic ureter.
Visceral afferents from the kidney and ureter enter about T11 to L2, which explains why ureteric colic is felt from loin to groin.
The short female urethra close to the perineum lets bowel flora such as uropathogenic Escherichia coli reach the bladder.

sections.title: Position of the kidneys and their posterior relations

blocks.text: The kidneys are retroperitoneal organs that lie in the paravertebral gutters on either side of the vertebral column, behind the parietal peritoneum and against the posterior abdominal wall. They extend from about T12 to L3. Each hilum faces anteromedially at about the level of L1, the transpyloric plane. Because the kidneys rest on the sloping psoas major, their upper poles lie closer to the midline and more posteriorly than their lower poles.

The right kidney lies slightly lower than the left because the large right lobe of the liver occupies the space above it. As a result the upper pole of the left kidney reaches about the 11th rib, while the upper pole of the right kidney lies at about the 12th rib. Each suprarenal gland caps the superomedial part of the upper pole.

The posterior relations are the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall and the diaphragm above them. The upper part of each kidney rests on the diaphragm, which separates it from the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura. Below the diaphragm the kidney lies on psoas major medially, quadratus lumborum in the middle, and the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis laterally. The subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run inferolaterally behind the kidney on these muscles.

blocks.text: These relations explain a standard examination finding. The costovertebral angle, between the 12th rib and the lateral border of the erector spinae, overlies the kidney. A distended, inflamed kidney, as in acute pyelonephritis or obstruction, stretches its capsule, and percussion at this angle jars it and provokes pain. The finding localizes disease to the kidney rather than to an intraperitoneal organ, because nothing intraperitoneal lies between the angle and the kidney.

sections.title: Anterior relations of the right and left kidneys

blocks.text: The organs in front of the kidneys differ on the two sides, and for each one it matters whether peritoneum separates it from the kidney. Secondarily retroperitoneal organs, such as the descending duodenum, the tail of the pancreas, and the colic flexures, lie directly on the kidney with no peritoneum between them. Intraperitoneal organs, such as the liver, stomach, spleen, and jejunum, are separated from the kidney by peritoneum and a potential space.

blocks.title: Anterior relations of the kidneys
rows: Right
Suprarenal gland (upper pole), descending duodenum (medially, near the hilum), right colic flexure (lower pole)
Liver (across the hepatorenal recess)
Left
Suprarenal gland (upper pole), tail of pancreas with splenic vessels (middle, near the hilum), left colic flexure and upper descending colon (lower lateral)
Stomach (across the omental bursa), spleen (upper lateral), jejunum (lower medial)
blocks.caption: Direct contacts are the routes by which disease or surgical injury passes between kidney and gut.

blocks.text: On the right, the hepatorenal recess lies between the liver and the peritoneum covering the kidney. In a supine patient it is the lowest point of the upper peritoneal cavity, so free blood or fluid collects there, and it is a standard view for detecting free fluid on bedside abdominal ultrasound. The descending duodenum lies directly on the medial part of the right kidney, close to the hilum, so a right renal mass, abscess, or operation can involve the duodenum.

On the left, the spleen lies against the upper lateral kidney, and the two are joined by the splenorenal ligament, which contains the splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail. A blow to the left flank therefore often injures the spleen and left kidney together. The pancreatic tail touches the left kidney directly, so pancreatic inflammation or tumor can spread into the anterior renal fascia. The stomach is separated from the kidney by the omental bursa, so disease of the posterior stomach wall spreads into the bursa or the pancreas rather than directly into the kidney.

The colon also explains a classic examination distinction. An enlarged kidney grows forward but stays behind the colon, so it is usually resonant to percussion over its front and can be balloted between the hands. An enlarged spleen grows forward and downward in front of the colon, so it is dull to percussion and has a palpable notch.

sections.title: Renal coverings and the structures at the hilum

blocks.text: Four layers surround each kidney, and they divide the area around it into compartments. These compartments decide where blood, pus, or urine collects.

blocks.title: Renal coverings, from the kidney outward
rows: Fibrous capsule
Thin, tough collagenous coat stripped easily from healthy kidney
Limits swelling, so a distended kidney stretches it and hurts; a subcapsular hematoma compresses the parenchyma
Perirenal (perinephric) fat
Fat directly around the kidney, continuous with the fat of the renal sinus
Cushions and helps hold the kidney in place; its loss allows the kidney to drop
Renal fascia (Gerota fascia)
Anterior and posterior membranous layers enclosing kidney, perirenal fat, and suprarenal gland
Forms the perirenal space that contains early renal bleeding or abscess
Pararenal (paranephric) fat
Fat outside the renal fascia, most abundant posteriorly
Separates the renal fascia from the posterior abdominal wall
blocks.caption: The renal fascia is the layer that defines the perirenal compartment.

blocks.text: Above and laterally, the two layers of renal fascia are fused, so the perirenal space is closed in those directions. Below, the layers are only loosely joined around the ureter. Blood or pus in the perirenal space is therefore held against the kidney at first, may displace it, and tends to track downward along the ureter toward the pelvis rather than upward. A thin septum of fascia separates the suprarenal gland from the kidney, and the gland is attached to the diaphragmatic crura. When rapid loss of perirenal fat lets the kidney descend (nephroptosis), the suprarenal gland stays in place, and the descending kidney can kink its ureter and cause intermittent obstruction.

The hilum opens into the renal sinus. From anterior to posterior the main hilar structures are the renal vein, the renal artery, and the renal pelvis. The pelvis is the most posterior, so it is the first hilar structure reached in a posterior approach, and the vein is the last. Branches of the artery often divide within the hilum, and a posterior segmental branch passes behind the pelvis, so the simple three-layer order describes the main trunks only.

The two sides differ in length. The left renal vein is long, crosses in front of the aorta just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. Compression between these two arteries raises pressure in the left gonadal vein, which is one explanation for left varicocele. The right renal artery is the longer artery and passes behind the inferior vena cava.

blocks.predict: A perirenal abscess forms around the right kidney. In which direction is the pus most likely to spread?
blocks.explain: Downward toward the pelvis along the ureter. The anterior and posterior layers of renal fascia are fused above and laterally but only loosely joined below, so the inferior side is the path of least resistance.

sections.title: Course of the ureter and the sites where stones lodge

blocks.text: Each ureter is a muscular tube about 25 to 30 cm long that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder by peristalsis. It has an abdominal part and a pelvic part of roughly equal length, and it is retroperitoneal throughout, adherent to the peritoneum on its front.

The abdominal ureter leaves the renal pelvis at the ureteropelvic junction and descends on the anterior surface of psoas major, roughly over the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, which is where it is looked for on a plain radiograph. The gonadal vessels cross in front of it. At the pelvic brim, near the sacroiliac joint, it passes over the bifurcation of the common iliac artery or the start of the external iliac artery. The pelvic ureter then runs down the lateral pelvic wall in front of the internal iliac artery, turns medially at about the level of the ischial spine, and reaches the bladder. In the male the ductus deferens crosses above it near the bladder; in the female the uterine artery crosses above it beside the cervix, where it can be injured during pelvic surgery. Finally it passes obliquely through the bladder wall to open at the ureteric orifice.

blocks.caption: A stone moves with peristalsis until the lumen is smaller than the stone.

blocks.text: The oblique intramural course works as a flap valve. As the bladder fills and contracts, rising pressure flattens the tunnel and stops urine from flowing back up the ureter. When the intramural segment is too short, as in primary vesicoureteral reflux, urine refluxes toward the kidney with each void, carrying bladder bacteria and predisposing to pyelonephritis and renal scarring.

blocks.title: Following a stone down the ureter
blocks.text: A 40-year-old man has severe colicky pain in the right flank that later moves to the right lower abdomen and groin. Hours later the pain reaches the tip of the penis and he feels urgent and frequent need to void. The first site, flank pain, fits obstruction at the ureteropelvic junction, which stretches the renal pelvis and capsule. Pain in the lower abdomen and groin places the stone near the pelvic brim. Urgency, frequency, and pain referred to the penis place it at the ureterovesical junction, where it irritates the trigone. Because this junction is the narrowest point, it is where a stone that has passed the other two most often stops.

blocks.predict: Why does a stone at the ureterovesical junction cause urgency and frequency, while a stone at the pelvic brim does not?
blocks.explain: At the ureterovesical junction the stone sits in the bladder wall beside the trigone. Irritation there stimulates bladder sensory nerves and produces the same sensation as a full bladder. At the pelvic brim the stone is far from the bladder.

sections.title: The bladder trigone and the male and female urethra

blocks.text: On the floor of the bladder, the trigone is the triangle with the two ureteric orifices at its upper corners and the internal urethral orifice at its lower apex. A ridge, the interureteric fold, joins the two ureteric orifices. The trigone is smooth whether the bladder is full or empty because its mucosa is bound firmly to the underlying muscle. The rest of the bladder lining is loosely attached and folds into rugae when the bladder is empty. The trigone also has a distinct developmental origin, forming where the lower ends of the mesonephric ducts are absorbed into the bladder wall.

In the male, smooth muscle around the bladder neck forms the internal urethral sphincter. Sympathetic contraction closes it during ejaculation so that semen passes forward and not back into the bladder. Behind the internal urethral orifice, the median lobe of the prostate raises a small bulge, the uvula, which enlarges with prostatic hyperplasia and can obstruct outflow.

blocks.text: The female urethra is only about 4 cm long. It runs from the bladder neck in front of the vagina, embedded in the anterior vaginal wall, and opens into the vestibule just in front of the vaginal orifice. This length and position explain why women have far more cystitis than men. Bowel organisms colonize the perineum and vaginal introitus, which sit only a few centimeters from the external urethral orifice, and they need to ascend only a short distance to reach the bladder. Sexual intercourse can push organisms into the urethra. In men the long urethra and the antibacterial activity of prostatic fluid add protection, and cystitis becomes common mainly with instrumentation or with outflow obstruction, such as prostatic enlargement, that leaves residual urine in the bladder.

sections.title: Male urethral injury: pelvic fracture versus straddle injury

blocks.text: The site of a urethral tear depends on where the urethra is fixed and on which bone it is pressed against. The membranous urethra is anchored by the external urethral sphincter and the perineal membrane, which spans the pubic arch. The prostate above it is attached to the pubis by the puboprostatic ligaments. The bulbous part of the spongy urethra lies below the perineal membrane, directly under the pubic arch.

In a pelvic fracture, displacement of the bony ring shears the prostate away from the fixed perineal membrane, and the posterior urethra tears at or near the membranous segment. Because the tear lies above the perineal membrane, blood and urine escape into the extraperitoneal retropubic and perivesical spaces of the pelvis rather than into the perineum. The detached prostate and bladder are lifted by the hematoma, so on rectal examination the prostate feels high-riding or cannot be felt. Typical findings are blood at the external meatus and inability to void despite a full bladder.

In a straddle injury, such as a fall astride a beam or bicycle bar, the bulbous urethra is crushed against the inferior pubic arch below the perineal membrane. If Buck fascia (the deep fascia of the penis) stays intact, blood and urine remain in a sleeve along the penile shaft. If Buck fascia tears, they enter the superficial perineal space beneath Colles fascia. This membranous layer continues into the scrotum, around the penis, and up the anterior abdominal wall as Scarpa fascia, so swelling spreads into those regions. It fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament and with the posterior edge of the perineal membrane, so the swelling does not reach the thighs or the anal triangle, and it produces a butterfly-shaped perineal bruise.

blocks.title: Localizing a urethral injury
blocks.text: Two men have blood at the urethral meatus. The first was crushed in a car and has an unstable pelvis; rectal examination finds a boggy mass and no palpable prostate, and the perineum looks normal. The prostate has been sheared off the fixed membranous urethra and lifted by a pelvic hematoma, so the tear is posterior and above the perineal membrane. The second fell onto a fence rail and has swelling of the scrotum, penis, and lower abdominal wall but none in the thighs. This pattern matches fluid confined by Colles and Scarpa fascia, so the tear is in the bulbous urethra below the perineal membrane, with Buck fascia torn.

integration.text: Development explains much of this anatomy. The kidneys develop from intermediate mesoderm behind the peritoneum in the pelvis and ascend to the lumbar region, so they remain retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall. A horseshoe kidney, whose fused lower poles are caught under the inferior mesenteric artery, stays low. The trigone arises from the absorbed mesonephric ducts, separately from the rest of the bladder wall. The duodenum, pancreas, and colon become fused to the posterior wall in front of the kidneys, which is why they touch the kidneys directly while the liver, stomach, and spleen stay separated by peritoneum.

Pathology follows the anatomy. Fascial compartments decide where perirenal blood or pus collects, narrow points decide where stones stop and what the kidney above them suffers, and a short urethra near the perineum decides who gets cystitis and with which organisms. Referred pain from the kidney and ureter follows the T11 to L2 spinal segments that their visceral afferents enter.

summary: The kidneys are retroperitoneal from about T12 to L3; the right kidney lies slightly lower than the left because of the liver.
Posteriorly each kidney rests on the diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis, with the subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves behind it.
The descending duodenum, pancreatic tail, and colic flexures touch the kidneys directly; the liver, stomach, spleen, and jejunum are separated by peritoneum.
The hepatorenal recess is the lowest part of the supine upper peritoneal cavity, where free fluid first collects.
The renal coverings from inside out are fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat; the renal fascia is closed above and laterally and open below.
At the hilum, from anterior to posterior, lie the renal vein, renal artery, and renal pelvis.

The ureter runs on psoas major behind the gonadal vessels and crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim; stones lodge at the ureteropelvic junction, pelvic brim, and ureterovesical junction, the narrowest.

The trigone is smooth because its mucosa is bound to the muscle; the male urethra is prostatic, membranous, and spongy, and the 4 cm female urethra explains the higher rate of ascending infection in women.
A pelvic fracture tears the membranous urethra above the perineal membrane, with a high-riding prostate and deep pelvic extravasation.
A straddle injury tears the bulbous urethra below the perineal membrane, with spread to the scrotum, penis, and abdominal wall but not the thighs.

verify: Vertebral levels (T12 to L3 for the kidneys, L1 for the hilum) and rib levels for the upper poles (11th on the left, 12th on the right) vary between sources and with respiration; confirm the levels NABNE expects.
Ureter length is quoted as 25 to 30 cm, intermediate (membranous) urethra as 1 to 2 cm, and total male urethra as 18 to 22 cm; values here are approximate.

Moore describes the membranous (intermediate) urethra as the narrowest part apart from the external urethral orifice, while some review sources call the membranous urethra simply the narrowest; confirm the wording NABNE uses.

Clinical series place the usual posterior urethral tear in pelvic fracture at the bulbomembranous junction rather than in the membranous segment itself; board sources teach the membranous urethra, which is used here.
The exact inferior and medial limits of the renal fascia and whether the perirenal spaces communicate across the midline are described differently in anatomical and radiological sources.
The spinal segments for renal and ureteric visceral afferents are given as about T11 to L2 here; some texts give T10 to L1 or T11 to L1.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Gerota fascia, Buck fascia, Colles fascia, Scarpa fascia, and Morison pouch, or only the descriptive terms.

Langman notes that the mesodermal lining of the trigone is later replaced by endodermal epithelium, and some newer work disputes a mesonephric origin for trigone muscle; the classic mesonephric origin is used here.
